performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
intro: “Der Lindenbaum” is the fifth song of Schubert’s Winterreise, D. 911, and concerns a linden tree by a well, linked with sweet dreams and with words carved into its bark. The piano depicts the rustling branches as the traveller passes the tree in the dark and is tempted by its offer of rest.

sections.label: Intro · Piano introduction in E major
sections.mNote: Fast, soft figures fill the three-beat bars.

sections.label: A · A tree beside the well
sections.mNote: The singer describes dreams and words cut into bark.

sections.label: B · Opening piano figure in E minor
sections.mNote: The opening piano figure returns in E minor.

sections.label: A′ · E major return, the tree’s invitation
sections.mNote: E major returns with the tree’s invitation.

sections.label: C · Cold wind; piano figures disturb E major
sections.mNote: Low C♮ and restless piano figures disturb E major.

sections.mNote: The opening tune returns softly in the major.

sections.label: Coda · The piano’s rustling figure returns
sections.mNote: The voice stops; the piano ends in E major.

cues.title: Piano introduction
cues.text: The piano plays fast figures for seven bars in E major before the singer enters. Schubert marks them pianississimo. Related piano figures return in the stanza about the cold wind.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, opening ppp, E-major signature and vocal pickup in bar 8; related piano figures recur in the cold-wind stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466. Müller’s text: https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-lindenbaum.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Linden tree by the well
cues.text: “Am Brunnen vor dem Tore”: by the well outside the gate. A linden tree stands there, and the traveller has many memories of it. He dreams in its shade, carves loving words into its bark and returns to it in joy and in sorrow.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Der Lindenbaum, first two stanzas, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation and paraphrase of the German at https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-lindenbaum. OpenScore Lieder, bars 8–24: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466.

cues.title: Third stanza in E minor
cues.text: The key signature changes to E minor at bar 25, and the third stanza begins at bar 28. The traveller passes the tree at night and closes his eyes, though it is already dark. The piano’s rustling figure, heard earlier in the major, is now in the minor.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, E-minor signature from bar 25 and third stanza from bar 28. Müller, third stanza: https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-lindenbaum. Score: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schober on “Der Lindenbaum”
cues.text: After Schubert sang the cycle to his friends, Schober said that of all the songs only “Der Lindenbaum” had pleased him. Schubert answered: “I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.”
cues.evidence: Joseph von Spaun’s recollection, quoted in Heinrich Welti’s article on Schubert, Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie 32 (1891), p. 626: Schober said “es habe ihm nur ein Lied darunter gefallen, nämlich der Lindenbaum”; Schubert replied “Mir gefallen diese Lieder mehr als alle anderen und sie werden Euch auch noch gefallen”. Translation ours. https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/ADB:Schubert,_Franz_(Komponist)

cues.title: Fifth stanza, bars 45–53
cues.text: At bar 45 a low C♮, marked fz, takes the piano away from E major. In the fifth stanza the cold wind blows into his face and blows his hat off. He sings “Ich wendete mich nicht” (I did not turn back) as the piano plays chromatic figures.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 45–53, low C♮ with fz and chromatic piano figures. Wilhelm Müller, Der Lindenbaum, fifth stanza, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation: https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-lindenbaum. Score: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final verse, major key
cues.text: The major-key tune returns at bar 58 for the final verse. The wanderer is now hours away, but he still hears the branches tell him “Du fändest Ruhe dort”, that he would find rest there. Schubert repeats this closing line through bar 76.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Der Lindenbaum, final stanza, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation: https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-lindenbaum. OpenScore Lieder, final verse from bar 58 and repeated closing line through bar 76: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano postlude, bars 77–82
cues.text: In the postlude (bars 77–82) the piano brings back the material of its introduction. It closes pp on a final chord of E major.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 77–82, piano postlude based on the introduction, pp and final E-major chord. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Rustling figure returns in E minor
transitions.from: A · A tree beside the well
transitions.to: B · Opening piano figure in E minor
transitions.how: The first two stanzas end in E major. At bar 25 the key signature changes to E minor, and the piano’s rustling figure returns with G♮ in place of G♯. The piano plays alone for three bars. The voice re-enters with a pickup in bar 28, as the traveller passes the tree in darkness.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 24–28: E-minor signature at bar 25 and vocal pickup at bar 28. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466

transitions.title: Return to E major, fourth stanza
transitions.from: B · Opening piano figure in E minor
transitions.to: A′ · E major return, the tree’s invitation
transitions.how: The voice goes straight on into the next stanza. At bar 37 the four-sharp signature returns, and the piano plays B–D♯–F♯, the dominant of E, as it sets the tree’s invitation. In Müller’s fourth stanza the branches offer the traveller rest.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 36–38: four-sharp signature returns at bar 37, with B–D♯–F♯ in the piano. Müller, fourth stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466; https://oxfordsong.org/song/der-lindenbaum

transitions.title: Low C at the cold-wind stanza
transitions.from: A′ · E major return, the tree’s invitation
transitions.to: C · Cold wind; piano figures disturb E major
transitions.how: In bars 45–53 the piano plays a low C♮, marked forzando (fz) in bars 45 and 47, against the E-major context. G♮ also enters the piano’s rapid figures. The voice moves from the smooth tune to the harsher phrases of the cold-wind stanza and takes up C♮.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 45–53: low C with fz in bars 45 and 47, G♮ in the piano and C♮ in the voice. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466

transitions.title: Piano interlude over a low B
transitions.from: C · Cold wind; piano figures disturb E major
transitions.to: A″ · Opening tune in the major
transitions.how: The voice stops, and the piano plays a four-bar interlude over a low B in the bass (bars 53–58). The rapid figures diminish under a diminuendo. The last stanza begins pianississimo, with the opening tune back in E major, as the traveller remembers the distant tree.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 53–58: bass B, diminuendo, four-bar interlude and ppp at the vocal return. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466

transitions.title: Final vocal E and piano postlude
transitions.from: A″ · Opening tune in the major
transitions.to: Coda · The piano’s rustling figure returns
transitions.how: The voice ends its repeated invitation to rest on E. The piano then takes up the fast figures of the introduction again, marked pianissimo, and plays them through to the final dominant–tonic cadence in E major, from a B-major chord to E major (bars 76–82).
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 76–82: vocal E, piano postlude marked pp, final B-major to E-major harmony. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5016466

source.title: Schubert, Winterreise No. 5, Der Lindenbaum, OpenScore Lieder transcription (CC0)
source.locator: Bars 1–82. Piano alone in bars 1–7, 25–27, 54–57 and 77–82. The opening rustling figure returns in the interludes and postlude.

timeline.note: Quiet, rapid figures in the piano represent the rustling branches.
The text tells of dreams under the tree and of words carved into its bark.
The rustling piano figure returns in E minor.
The singer passes the tree in darkness, hears its call and turns into the cold wind.
Four bars of piano over a low B subside towards the last stanza.
The last stanza repeats the tree’s invitation to rest three times.
The piano’s opening figure returns and closes in E major.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The recording appears to sing all six strophes; no source consulted states the performing text or the key of the transfer. Utz classifies recordings by transposition from the first edition, but the value for this song and the absolute pitch of the transfer are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Gramola Record (The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited), as printed on the scanned copy
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows a Gramola Record imprint, whereas the photographed first disc carries the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ES 384, and the Commons file name and the Internet Archive description agree.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CK 2950, take 2 (run-out “Ck 2950” with II); side No. 5 (label number 0942028); reverse side: Wasserflut (matrix CK 2951-2). Disc 3 of 12 of the set; 30 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (256.00 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (255.88 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.

composer.epithet: Composer who at seventeen wrote a song for Gretchen with a spinning-wheel accompaniment and at thirty-one wrote music for two cellos.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola, his brothers the violins and his father the cello. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer taught him further. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where he played Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven in the school orchestra.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. In the piano part the right hand imitates the spinning wheel and the left hand the treadle, while Goethe’s Gretchen sings of her thoughts of Faust. At the point where she recalls his kiss, the accompaniment figure stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
